newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Hardliners move ahead in Bosnian election.
newsitem.headline: Hardliners move ahead in Bosnian election.

text.p: Bosnia's first elections after a savage 43-month-long war seemed set on Tuesday to hand victory to communal hardliners -- leaving rival moderates far behind.

In vote counting for the top job in a joint Bosnian presidency, hardline Serb nationalist Momcilo Krajisnik has also made big gains on Moslem Alija Izetbegovic, according to unofficial election tallies obtained on Tuesday.
The election is the main plank of U.S.-led efforts to reintegrate the shattered country and mend deep wounds caused by ethnic cleansing, mass rape, massacre and counter-massacre.
But critics of the poll say separatist ambitions, unresolved border disputes and the re-arming of old foes suggest conflict, not peace, lies ahead if nationalists emerge victorious.

Both unofficial and official OSCE figures released on Tuesday showed Izetbegovic with a lead of roughly 80 percent to 14 percent over his opposition rival for the Moslem seat on the presidency, ex-prime minister and moderate Haris Silajdzic.
Krajisnik was also far ahead of his Serb opposition rival for the presidency, with about 78 percent of the vote compared to 19 percent for centrist Mladen Ivanic.
In the race for the Croat seat on the presidency, nationalist Kresimir Zubak staked out a wide margin, 87 percent to 11 percent for moderate competitor Ivo Komsic.

In the presidential contest, Izetbegovic's lead over the ultra-nationalist speaker of the current Bosnian Serb assembly had narrowed from 29 percent to 20 percent overnight with fewer than half the votes counted, the unofficial figures from Saturday's general elections indicated.
Although the three-man Bosnian presidency will rule by consensus, the candidate who wins the most votes will be the senior member who will represent the country abroad.
A hardline Serb winning this position would be a major blow for the Moslems who represent the country's largest community.

Diplomats close to the counting conducted by the OSCE said Izetbegovic, the Bosnian president, had 268,000 votes with 40 of 80 counting centres accounted for in Bosnian Federation territory, where only Moslem and Croat candidates ran.
Krajisnik, ultra-nationalist speaker of the current Bosnian Serb republic assembly, had surged to 214,000 votes with 26 of 72 precincts reporting from the Serb entity, they told Reuters.

The sources emphasised that the figures, although more comprehensive than the official OSCE computer total released so far, were preliminary and could change somewhat once they were audited and re-checked according to OSCE rules.
But they said there was little doubt Krajisnik was drawing closer to Izetbegovic, noting a greater number of counting centres in Serb territory had yet to report than in the Federation.

A Krajisnik victory in the presidency sweepstakes could pose big obstacles to rebuilding joint governing bodies in Bosnia because his Serb nationalist party seeks "independence" for the half of the country where it rules.
Izetbegovic's SDA party, though Moslem nationalist in tone, is formally committed to Bosnia's reintegration and a return of war refugees to their homes, in stark contrast with the Serbs.

The tripartite body, envisaged to govern for two years until Bosnia's next elections planned in 1998, will also include one Croat. Critics say the plan for government by consensus is a recipe for paralysis.
Although Izetbegovic clung to a good lead, a victory was by no means assured for several reasons.

Many tens of thousands of Moslem refugees, natural SDA supporters, registered to vote in Serb territory in hopes of regaining their homes sooner. But only Serbs were listed on the presidential ballot in Serb territory.
That factor, as well as the possibility Silajdzic would siphon away Moslem votes crucial to Izetbegovic, could put Krajisnik in the driver's seat in the final counting.
Western diplomats told Reuters Izetbegovic was still in a strong position because Siljadzic was not doing as well as expected in his supposed urban strongholds.
Moreover, Krajisnik's support is weakest in northwest Bosnia where the majority of Bosnian Serbs live.
Initial results from voting for a new inter-communal Bosnian parliament are not expected until mid-week.

The United States said it would work with Bosnia's election victors over the next month or so to establish new joint governing bodies, reversing the wartime partition of the country, and then focus on whether NATO forces should remain.
